summary: Describes the use of HDLC-like framing for PPP encapsulated packets. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1662 defines how PPP frames are marked and checked on point-to-point links. It also explains how senders alter special byte or bit patterns so they cannot be mistaken for frame markers.

questions: what is the ppp flag sequence 0x7e
how does ppp escape control characters
what is the ppp async control character map
subtitle: How PPP marks frame boundaries and protects its data on serial and synchronous links.

tldr.problem: A point-to-point link needs a way to mark where each PPP frame begins and ends, carry special byte values, and detect transmission errors.
tldr.mechanism: HDLC-like framing uses flag sequences, fixed address and control fields, a Frame Check Sequence, and octet or bit stuffing for transparency.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1662 is Internet Standard STD 51 and obsoletes RFC 1549.

today: RFC 1662 is Internet Standard STD 51 and obsoletes RFC 1549.

sections.title: Link Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 1662 describes HDLC-like framing for PPP packets over bit-oriented and octet-oriented synchronous links, and asynchronous links with 8 data bits and no parity. Links MUST be full duplex, so both endpoints can transmit at the same time. The circuit may be dedicated or circuit-switched.

The physical layer presents an octet interface to PPP and must transparently carry PPP frames. PPP does not set a transmission-rate limit and does not require control signals such as RTS or CTS.
sections.plainLanguage: The link must let both endpoints transmit and must carry PPP frames without changing them. PPP does not require a particular transmission speed.

sections.title: The Frame Layout
sections.content:
A basic frame contains a Flag, Address, Control, Protocol, Information, optional Padding, Frame Check Sequence (FCS), and another Flag. The flag is the bit pattern 01111110, or 0x7e. Address is 0xff and Control is 0x03; the Protocol, Information, and Padding fields are defined by PPP.

The FCS is 16 bits by default, with a 32-bit version also defined for negotiation. It covers the Address, Control, Protocol, Information, and Padding fields, but not the flags or the FCS itself. Link Control Protocol can negotiate omission of the Address and Control fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame has a marker at each end and a check value near the end. The receiver uses the markers to find the frame and the check value to detect errors.

sections.title: Octet Stuffing on Byte Links
sections.content:
On asynchronous and octet-synchronous links, the sender escapes each flag, each Control Escape octet, and each control character selected by the sending map. It replaces the octet with 0x7d followed by the original octet XORed with 0x20. At minimum, senders MUST escape the flag and Control Escape values, and receivers MUST process escape sequences.

On receipt, the receiver removes any mapped control characters inserted by intervening equipment and reverses the escape operation before computing the FCS. A frame that ends with an escape immediately followed by a flag is discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: On byte-based links, special bytes are sent as an escape byte followed by an altered value. The receiver reverses that change before checking the frame.

sections.title: Bit Stuffing on Synchronous Links
sections.content:
On bit-synchronous links, the sender inserts a zero after every sequence of five consecutive one bits in the frame, including the FCS. This prevents data from accidentally containing the flag pattern. The receiver removes the inserted zero before checking the FCS.

Frames shorter than 4 octets with a 16-bit FCS, or frames ending with more than six consecutive one bits, are silently discarded. The RFC recommends NRZ as the default line encoding at the stated common speeds and recommends negotiating a 32-bit FCS when NRZI is used.
sections.plainLanguage: On bit-based links, the sender inserts a zero after five consecutive one bits. This keeps the data from looking like the frame marker.

sections.title: Negotiating Control Characters
sections.content:
The Async-Control-Character-Map (ACCM) is a Link Control Protocol option that identifies control characters that must remain escaped on asynchronous links. Each end keeps a 32-bit receiving map and a sending map that may be up to 256 bits. The option is Type 2 and Length 6.

For asynchronous links, the default map is 0xffffffff; for other link types, it is zero. A set bit means the matching octet MUST remain mapped. Synchronous implementations MUST acknowledge the ACCM option because a converter may perform the mapping.
sections.plainLanguage: The two endpoints can agree which control bytes need escaping. A converter between link types may handle that escaping for a synchronous endpoint.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The link layer may not learn that the physical connection has changed. The RFC warns that relying on the security of switching systems in that situation can allow an insertion attack to go undetected or let an attacker spoof the calling identity to avoid link authentication.

The physical layer guidance recommends signalling a Down event when enough time has passed since a disconnection. The RFC notes that choosing faster setup can reduce security.
sections.plainLanguage: If a physical connection changes without notice, the link may not recognize that a different party is connected. Signalling a disconnected link can reduce this risk.
